name: Professional Learning That Works
title: Professional Learning That Works
answer: Professional learning about AI works best when it builds teachers' knowledge of how to teach with AI rather than their technical skill alone. Research on teachers and students shows that pedagogical knowledge, not tool fluency, predicts how students value AI and want to learn about it. This means training should be ongoing, tied to real lessons, and grounded in practice rather than one-off tool demonstrations.

sections.body: This idea says that professional learning about AI should focus on teaching with AI, not just on how to operate tools. The problem it solves is that schools often invest in technical training that does not change classroom practice or student outcomes. Research suggests technical knowledge by itself can even slightly lower students' views of AI's social value. What matters instead is teachers' understanding of how to use AI for teaching, which is what builds confidence and student interest. Pedagogy comes first, technology second.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, this looks like teachers applying AI to their own lessons rather than learning tools in the abstract. Teachers who practiced with their own material grew more than those who studied tools in isolation. One promising approach is case based learning, where teachers work through realistic cases of AI in teaching that range from simple to messy, and the messier cases push them to apply what they learned. The text describes this approach with middle school science teachers, and it fits the broader research. Professional learning should also be ongoing rather than a single day, giving teachers time to try tools, reflect, and share with colleagues, with professional learning communities as a natural home for the work.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea as supported by research. A study of 46 secondary teachers and more than 2,800 students found that teachers' knowledge of how to teach with AI, not their technical skill, predicted students' views of AI's value for society and their interest in learning about it (Shen et al., 2026), and technical knowledge alone slightly lowered students' views of AI's social value. A study of 325 teachers in 26 countries found that the path from technical skill to confident use of AI in teaching ran through teachers' knowledge of how to use technology for teaching (Mohebi & ElSayary, 2026). A program with middle school science teachers found that working through realistic cases of AI in teaching, from simple to messy, raised teachers' AI literacy, and the messier cases pushed teachers to apply what they learned (Ding et al., 2024). The text notes that this last study was small but that its approach fits the broader research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets out limits and risks around how professional learning is designed and sustained. A district that offers one training and expects lasting change will be disappointed, so leaders must commit to ongoing time for teachers to try tools, reflect, and share. Technical knowledge alone is not enough and can slightly lower students' views of AI's social value, so pedagogy must lead. The case based study was small, so its findings should be read alongside the broader research rather than as proof on their own. Decisions about what teachers learn, how cases are chosen, and how professional learning communities are used stay with school leaders and teachers, not with the tools themselves.
